The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The first post covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The second scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we introduced last month . Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( GB300 source ). We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. items.title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
items.summary: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

items.title: CastWorld: Benchmarking Context-Aware Agentic Time Series Forecasting Beyond Predictive Accuracy
items.summary: Agentic time series forecasting extends conventional approaches beyond one-shot numerical prediction toward autonomous, context-aware interaction. However, existing benchmarks offer limited integrated support for diverse contextual information, forecasting-specific adaptive interactions, and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents. In this paper, we introduce CastWorld, an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting. First, its context-rich dataset suite spans 8 domains and 25 real-world datasets, covering external variables, events, and historical cases under a unified context specification. Second, a lightweight, modular forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions and enables iterative evidence gathering and forecast revision. Intermediate forecasts can expose information gaps, while newly acquired evidence guides subsequent revisions and final version selection. Third, model-level evaluation assesses forecast quality, process execution, behavioral trustworthiness, and resource efficiency through decision trajectories and forecast-version histories. Also, systems-level evaluation compares predictive accuracy across forecasting systems. Experiments reveal distinct decision behaviors among agents with comparable accuracy. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best previously generated predictions. Allowing evidence acquisition during forecast refinement improves task-aware forecast scores across all three evaluated models. CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic time series forecasting under controlled conditions.

items.title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
items.summary: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. items.content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. items.story_key: story|title:kitesurf is now open source
items.content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. items.title: claude-code v2.1.323
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
  • Added engines["claude-code"] to plugin.json: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
  • Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to claude plugin validate; each finding is a warning, and --strict fails on it
  • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces
  • Added support for CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide
  • Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a * in a variable's value, such as Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)
  • Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
  • Added a one-time startup notice naming CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES (available since 2.1.318): set it to 1 to turn off subagent progress summaries and the requests that write them (#86879)
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_HINT_COMMAND, which a program that starts Claude Code can set to have the exit hint name its own resume command
  • Added unsetOptionCount to the claude plugin install --json result: how many userConfig options are not yet set
  • Added isPromptCovered to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt
  • Fixed running /compact again, or after a command such as /context, summarizing away a message that Claude had not answered yet
  • Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
  • Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
  • Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to settings.json moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
  • Fixed claude plugin commands and claude mcp list signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed
  • Fixed Edit and Bash running out of memory on certain /proc files, and Edit hanging or running out of memory on devices and named pipes
  • Fixed Claude Code failing to start, or to clear stored credentials at sign-out, when saving its configuration file failed with "Out of memory"
  • Fixed requests sent without streaming failing on errors that streamed requests recover from, such as a rejected image, thinking block or beta header
  • Fixed ExitWorktree, the worktree exit dialog and /resume leaving the session in the wrong folder when the folder the shell was in before entering the worktree had been deleted
  • Fixed accents and other combining marks sometimes landing left of the text, leaving stale copies on screen, or silently disappearing when text wraps
  • Fixed the last key of a key chord, such as Enter in ctrl+x enter, acting on a dialog's text field when the chord's own action isn't available there
  • Fixed ps processes piling up when the process listing Claude Code runs before stopping a command takes too long

  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed the Stop button disappearing from a cloud session five minutes into a reply that had shown nothing yet while Claude was still working
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed an approval prompt sometimes disappearing from a tab left open after a self-hosted runner released the session while it waited for your answer
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a failure notification when a scheduled task's run can't start because its settings require a sandbox that isn't available where it runs
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the Git providers page when your GitHub sign-in has expired: it now asks you to reconnect instead of silently hiding organizations you can link
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed removing a repository from a scheduled task silently moving its GitHub trigger to another repository; Save now waits until you pick one
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed git clones and fetches that take longer than ten minutes in a cloud session sometimes being cut off at the very end
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added the No repository option to the repository picker for new sessions on a self-hosted environment
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a warning to a cloud session's Delete dialog when deleting it will pause scheduled tasks that run in that session

  • [Claude Tag] Fixed scheduled tasks in a Slack channel moved between Enterprise Grid workspaces failing to use Slack until someone posted there
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Approve and post card in a DM with Claude appearing for private or Slack Connect channels, where Claude can't post; Claude now gets the reason and shows no card
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Retry button to a Slack channel's Configure page for when its settings fail to load
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Scope filter to the Network events tab of Claude Tag's Activity page, so admins can download one scope's events instead of the whole organization's
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Remove connector in Claude Tag admin settings being refused when access bundles also held its credentials; it now removes those set on the connector and leaves the bundles' own
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Channels tab in Claude Tag admin settings splitting a workspace from its channels across pages; channels now appear right under their workspace
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Set for Claude Tag link on the Cloud environments admin page not leading to the environment setting; it now opens the Slack page's Advanced tab, where you set it
  • [Code Review] Added a Download CSV button to Code Review admin settings: export review costs per repository by month, week or day, for one repository, one GitHub organization or all
